hero.title: Website load time: why performance matters for users and businesses
hero.intro: Load time isn't a purely technical detail for developers — it's one of the few website properties that visitors feel directly and Google measures directly.

keyTakeaway.title: In short
keyTakeaway.text: Google evaluates load time, interactivity and visual stability through what it calls Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS). Google treats these as a ranking signal — one of many, not the decisive one. Content relevance still matters more, but between otherwise comparable pages, performance can tip the balance.

sections.heading: What Core Web Vitals actually measure
paragraphs: Core Web Vitals are three concrete, measurable values Google uses to assess a website's user experience:
checklist: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — how fast the largest visible element on the page loads. Under 2.5 seconds is considered good.
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — how quickly the page responds to a user interaction. Under 200 milliseconds is considered good.
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — how much content shifts unexpectedly while the page loads. Under 0.1 is considered good.

sections.heading: Why this is something visitors actually feel
paragraphs: These values aren't abstract technical metrics — they describe exactly what a visitor experiences as "slow" or "janky": waiting for content, a delayed response after clicking, a button shifting right before you meant to tap it.

That last point is often underestimated: a layout that keeps shifting while it loads causes visitors to accidentally tap the wrong element — an ad instead of the intended button, the wrong menu item instead of the contact page. That doesn't just cost patience — in the worst case, it costs you an enquiry outright.

sections.heading: How Google actually uses these values
paragraphs: Google doesn't measure Core Web Vitals in a lab — it uses real visitor data from the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). A page is considered "good" when at least 75 percent of real visits meet the thresholds above.

Core Web Vitals are part of what Google calls page-experience signals and are a confirmed ranking factor. The important context: content relevance remains the stronger signal. Performance matters most where several pages are otherwise similarly relevant — that's where it can tip the scale.

sections.heading: Why performance matters even without Google in the picture
paragraphs: Even setting the ranking signal aside entirely, a simple point remains: a slow website directly costs you visitors. Someone who clicks an ad or a search result and then waits several seconds for a responsive page will often just leave — before ever seeing what you actually offer.
Performance is therefore both an SEO topic and a pure conversion topic: a faster website loses fewer visitors on the way to the actual action, regardless of how they found you.

sections.heading: What this means practically for your business
paragraphs: You don't need to understand the technical details yourself to ask an important question: does whoever builds your website actually pay attention to load time, image optimisation and technical structure — or is performance an afterthought? That question is worth asking in the very first conversation with any agency or freelancer.

A simple, free first check: Google offers PageSpeed Insights, a public tool that shows the current Core Web Vitals values for any website — a good starting point to assess your own site objectively rather than relying on a subjective feeling.
